% ================================================================
% An introduction to surds.
%
% A first sheet on surds for a lower ability Year 10 class, designed
% to be worked through with the calculator on the desk. Surds are
% met first as square roots whose decimals never end. Pupils then
% work out a mixed list of surds and multiples of surds on the
% calculator and spot which of them are equal, which leads into the
% rule for simplifying surds. Adding and subtracting surds is built
% on collecting like terms in algebra, and multiplying and dividing
% surds is taught straight from the formulas, with the formulas for
% each part boxed. The sheet ends with "many ways to make a surd"
% diagrams: one worked example, then diagrams with less and less
% filled in. Answers are on the last page.
%
% The sheet is written on, so every question is followed by a
% working area. The \newpage commands in the body are placed so that
% no question is split across the fold.
% ================================================================

\pagestyle{empty}
\linespread{1.15}\selectfont
\setlength{\parskip}{5pt}
\setlist[enumerate,1]{label=\textbf{Q\arabic*.}, leftmargin=*, itemsep=10pt, topsep=6pt, parsep=4pt}
\setlist[enumerate,2]{label=(\alph*), leftmargin=*, itemsep=8pt, topsep=5pt, parsep=3pt}
\setlength{\multicolsep}{4pt}
\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}

\newcommand{\ansline}[1][2.2cm]{\underline{\hspace{#1}}}
% A short gap for a single number, sized to sit inside a line of maths.
\newcommand{\gap}{\underline{\hspace{0.7cm}}}
% A gap under a root sign. An underline leaves too little room beneath the
% radical, so a faint dotted box marks where the number is written instead.
% The box is the tallest that still keeps the ordinary-sized root sign,
% and is measured in em so that it scales with the type around it.
\newcommand{\rootgap}{\tikz[baseline=0pt]\draw[gray!60,densely dotted,thick]
  (0,-0.12em) rectangle (1.8em,0.83em);}

\tikzset{fnkey/.style={draw=black!75,fill=black!75,text=white,rounded corners=2.5pt,
    font=\small\bfseries,minimum height=6mm,minimum width=9mm,inner sep=2pt},
  nmkey/.style={fnkey,draw=black!45,fill=black!8,text=black}}
\newcommand{\calckey}[1]{\tikz[baseline=(k.base)]\node[fnkey] (k) {#1};}
\newcommand{\numkey}[1]{\tikz[baseline=(k.base)]\node[nmkey] (k) {#1};}
\newcommand{\sqrtkey}{\calckey{$\sqrt{\blacksquare}$}}
\newcommand{\sdkey}{\calckey{S$\Leftrightarrow$D}}
\newcommand{\calcscreen}[2]{%
  \tikz[baseline=(s.center)]{%
    \node[draw=black!60,fill=teal!6!gray!12,rounded corners=2pt,
      minimum width=3.7cm,minimum height=1.3cm] (s) {};
    \node[anchor=north west,font=\small] at ([xshift=3pt,yshift=-2pt]s.north west) {#1};
    \node[anchor=south east,font=\small] at ([xshift=-4pt,yshift=3pt]s.south east) {#2};}}

% ----------------------------------------------------------------
% A "many ways to make" diagram: a surd in the middle, joined to five
% boxes that each hold a calculation whose answer is that surd.
% \spider{<middle>}{<addition>}{<subtraction>}{<multiplication>}
%        {<division>}{<single square root>}
% Any box, or the middle, can be left empty for pupils to fill in.
\newcommand{\spiderbox}[4]{%
  \node[draw=blue!45!black,rounded corners=3pt,thick,fill=white,
    minimum width=3.0cm,minimum height=1.15cm] (#1) at (#2) {};
  \node[font=\scriptsize\itshape,text=gray!70!black,anchor=north,inner sep=2pt]
    at (#1.north) {#3};
  \node[font=\small] at ([yshift=-0.12cm]#1.center) {#4};
  \draw[gray,thick] (m) -- (#1);}
\newcommand{\spider}[6]{%
  \begin{tikzpicture}[baseline=(current bounding box.north)]
    \node[draw=green!35!black,fill=green!8,circle,thick,minimum size=1.3cm,
      inner sep=1pt,font=\large] (m) at (0,0) {#1};
    \spiderbox{sa}{0,2.2}{an addition}{#2}
    \spiderbox{ss}{2.45,0.55}{a subtraction}{#3}
    \spiderbox{sm}{1.65,-1.85}{a multiplication}{#4}
    \spiderbox{sd}{-1.65,-1.85}{a division}{#5}
    \spiderbox{sr}{-2.45,0.55}{a single square root}{#6}
  \end{tikzpicture}}

\begin{document}

\begin{center}
  {\Large\bfseries \ealpara{Wprowadzenie do \ealkeytr{pierwiastków niewymiernych}}{An Introduction to \ealkey{Surds}}}
\end{center}

\begin{keyidea}
\ealpara{\textbf{\ealkeytr{Pierwiastek niewymierny}} to \ealkeytr{pierwiastek}, którego nie można zapisać dokładnie w postaci \ealkeytr{liczby całkowitej nieujemnej} lub \ealkeytr{ułamka}, taki jak $\sqrt{2}$.}{A \textbf{\ealkey{surd}} is a \ealkey{square root} that cannot be written exactly as a \ealkey{whole number} or a \ealkey{fraction}, such as $\sqrt{2}$.}
\end{keyidea}

\parttitle{1}{\ealkey{Square roots} on the calculator}

\ealpara{\ealkeytr{Pierwiastek} liczby to liczba, która daje tę liczbę, gdy pomnoży się ją przez siebie. Na przykład $\sqrt{9}=3$, ponieważ $3\times3=9$.}{The \textbf{\ealkey{square root}} of a number is the number that gives it when it is multiplied by itself. For example $\sqrt{9}=3$, because $3\times3=9$.}

\ealpara{Aby znaleźć \ealkeytr{pierwiastek} na kalkulatorze, wciskamy przycisk \ealkeytr{pierwiastka}, wpisujemy liczbę i wciskamy równa się. Wiele kalkulatorów podaje odpowiedź jako \ealkeytr{pierwiastek niewymierny}. Aby zobaczyć odpowiedź jako \ealkeytr{ułamek dziesiętny}, wciśnij przycisk S$\Leftrightarrow$D.}{To find a \ealkey{square root} on the calculator we press the \ealkey{square root} button, type the number and press equals. Many calculators give the answer as a \ealkey{surd}. To see the answer as a \ealkey{decimal}, press the S$\Leftrightarrow$D button.}

\vspace{4pt}
\begin{center}
\sqrtkey\;\numkey{7}\;\calckey{$=$}
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\calcscreen{$\sqrt{7}$}{$\sqrt{7}$}
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\sdkey
\quad$\longrightarrow$\quad
\calcscreen{$\sqrt{7}$}{$2.645751311$}
\end{center}
\vspace{2pt}

\ealpara{Kalkulator pokazuje $\sqrt{7}=2.645751311$, ale \ealkeytr{ułamek dziesiętny} nie kończy się na krawędzi ekranu. Ciągnie się w nieskończoność, więc zamiast tego piszemy $\sqrt{7}$.}{The calculator shows $\sqrt{7}=2.645751311$, but the \ealkey{decimal} does not stop at the edge of the screen. It carries on forever, so we write $\sqrt{7}$ instead.}

\begin{enumerate}

\item \ealpara{Użyj przycisku \ealkeytr{pierwiastka}, aby uzupełnić tabelę. Gdy odpowiedź nie jest \ealkeytr{liczbą całkowitą nieujemną}, \ealkeytr{obcinaj} do pierwszych czterech \ealkeytr{miejsc dziesiętnych}.}{Use the \ealkey{square root} button to complete the table. When the answer is not a \ealkey{whole number}, \ealkey{truncate} to the first four \ealkey{decimal places}.}

\ealpara{Kolumny tabeli: \ealkeytr{pierwiastek}; odpowiedź kalkulatora; czy to \ealkeytr{pierwiastek niewymierny}?}{Table columns: \ealkey{square root}; calculator answer; is it a \ealkey{surd}?}

\vspace{2pt}
\begin{center}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}
\begin{tabular}{|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{2.6cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{5.2cm}|>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{3.4cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{\ealkey{Square root}} & \textbf{Calculator answer} & \textbf{Is it a \ealkey{surd}?}\\
\hline
$\sqrt{16}$ & $4$ & No\\ \hline
$\sqrt{2}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{49}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{3}$ & & \\ \hline
$\sqrt{10}$ & & \\ \hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\end{enumerate}

\newpage

\parttitle{2}{\ealkey{Surds} that are equal}

\ealpara{$3\sqrt{2}$ oznacza $3\times\sqrt{2}$, czyli trzy razy $\sqrt{2}$, tak samo jak $3x$ oznacza $3\times x$ w \ealkeytr{algebrze}. Aby znaleźć $3\sqrt{2}$, wciskamy \numkey{3}\;\sqrtkey\;\numkey{2}\;\calckey{$=$} na kalkulatorze.}{$3\sqrt{2}$ means $3\times\sqrt{2}$, which is three lots of $\sqrt{2}$, in the same way that $3x$ means $3\times x$ in \ealkey{algebra}. To find $3\sqrt{2}$ we press \numkey{3}\;\sqrtkey\;\numkey{2}\;\calckey{$=$} on the calculator.}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \ealpara{Użyj kalkulatora, aby znaleźć każdą odpowiedź, \ealkeytr{obciętą} do czterech \ealkeytr{miejsc dziesiętnych}.}{Use your calculator to find each answer, \ealkey{truncated} to four \ealkey{decimal places}.}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{\arabic*.},itemsep=14pt]
  \item $2\sqrt{2}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{12}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{6}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{18}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{20}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $2\sqrt{3}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $\sqrt{8}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $3\sqrt{5}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $2\sqrt{5}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
  \item $3\sqrt{2}=\ansline[3.5cm]$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

  \item \ealpara{Cztery pary liczb w części (a) są sobie równe. Zapisz te cztery pary w postaci \ealkeytr{pierwiastka niewymiernego}. Dwie liczby nie mają pary.}{Four pairs of numbers in part (a) are equal to each other. Write down the four pairs, in \ealkey{surd} form. Two of the numbers do not have a partner.}

\vspace{8pt}
\begin{multicols}{2}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\vspace{14pt}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]

\vspace{14pt}
\ansline[2.5cm] $=$ \ansline[2.5cm]
\end{multicols}
\end{enumerate}

\end{enumerate}

\vspace{6pt}
\ealpara{Pary w zadaniu 2 są równe, ponieważ możemy wyłączyć \ealkeytr{liczbę kwadratową} jako \ealkeytr{dzielnik}. Na przykład $8=4\times2$, a $\sqrt{4}=2$, więc $\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$. Zapisywanie $\sqrt{8}$ jako $2\sqrt{2}$ nazywa się \ealkeytr{uproszczeniem} \ealkeytr{pierwiastka niewymiernego}.}{The pairs in Q2 are equal because we can \ealkey{factor} out a \ealkey{square number}. For example $8=4\times2$, and $\sqrt{4}=2$, so $\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{2}=2\sqrt{2}$. Writing $\sqrt{8}$ as $2\sqrt{2}$ is called \textbf{\ealkey{simplifying}} the \ealkey{surd}.}

\begin{formulas}{\ealkey{simplifying} \ealkey{surds}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{5.2cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{a\times b}=\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}$
  & for example \; $\sqrt{20}=\sqrt{4\times5}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{5}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
\ealpara{Słownie: rozdziel liczbę pod \ealkeytr{pierwiastkiem} na \ealkeytr{liczbę kwadratową} pomnożoną przez inną liczbę. \ealkeytr{Pierwiastek} z \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej} zapisuje się przed \ealkeytr{pierwiastkiem niewymiernym}.}{In words: split the number under the \ealkey{root} into a \ealkey{square number} multiplied by another number. The \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number} is written in front of the \ealkey{surd}.}

\vspace{4pt}
\ealkey{Square numbers}: \; $4$, \; $9$, \; $16$, \; $25$, \; $36$, \; $49$, \; $64$,
\; $81$, \; $100$
\end{formulas}

\newpage

\begin{wex}{\ealkey{simplify} $\sqrt{18}$}
\small
\ealpara{Krok 1 --- rozdziel liczbę, używając \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}. Krok 2 --- rozdziel \ealkeytr{pierwiastek}. Krok 3 --- oblicz \ealkeytr{pierwiastek} z \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}.}{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}. Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}. Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9\times2}$\\[8pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}.} & $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}$\\[8pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{18}=3\times\sqrt{2}=3\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \ealpara{Uzupełnij luki w podpunktach (a) i (b), a następnie \ealkeytr{uprość} podpunkty (c) do (h) w ten sam sposób.}{Fill in the gaps in parts (a) and (b), then \ealkey{simplify} parts (c) to (h) in the same way.}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \ealpara{\ealkeytr{Uprość} $\sqrt{12}$.}{\ealkey{Simplify} $\sqrt{12}$.}

\vspace{2pt}
{\small
\ealpara{Krok 1 --- rozdziel liczbę, używając \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}. Krok 2 --- rozdziel \ealkeytr{pierwiastek}. Krok 3 --- oblicz \ealkeytr{pierwiastek} z \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}.}{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}. Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}. Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{12}=\sqrt{\rootgap\times3}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}.} & $\sqrt{12}=\sqrt{\rootgap}\times\sqrt{3}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{12}=\gap\times\sqrt{3}=\gap\sqrt{3}$\\
\end{tabular}}

  \item \ealpara{\ealkeytr{Uprość} $\sqrt{50}$.}{\ealkey{Simplify} $\sqrt{50}$.}

\vspace{2pt}
{\small
\ealpara{Krok 1 --- rozdziel liczbę, używając \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}. Krok 2 --- rozdziel \ealkeytr{pierwiastek}. Krok 3 --- oblicz \ealkeytr{pierwiastek} z \ealkeytr{liczby kwadratowej}.}{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}. Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}. Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
\begin{tabular}[b]{@{}l@{\hspace{1.2em}}l@{}}
\textbf{Step 1 --- split the number using a \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{50}=\sqrt{\rootgap\times\rootgap}$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 2 --- split the \ealkey{root}.} & $\sqrt{50}=\ansline[3.5cm]$\\[12pt]
\textbf{Step 3 --- take the \ealkey{square root} of the \ealkey{square number}.}
  & $\sqrt{50}=\ansline[3.5cm]$\\
\end{tabular}}
\end{enumerate}
\begin{multicols}{3}
\begin{enumerate}[resume]
  \item $\sqrt{24}$
  \item $\sqrt{28}$
  \item $\sqrt{45}$
  \item $\sqrt{63}$
  \item $\sqrt{75}$
  \item $\sqrt{98}$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

\end{enumerate}

\parttitle{3}{Adding and subtracting \ealkey{surds}}

\begin{enumerate}[resume]

\item \ealpara{\textbf{Rozgrzewka.} \ealkeytr{Uprość} każde \ealkeytr{wyrażenie}, dodając \ealkeytr{wyrazy podobne}. Jeśli \ealkeytr{wyrażenia} nie można \ealkeytr{uprościć}, zapisz je tak, jak jest.}{\textbf{Warm-up.} \ealkey{Simplify} each \ealkey{expression} by collecting \ealkey{like terms}. If an \ealkey{expression} cannot be \ealkey{simplified}, write it as it is.}
\begin{multicols}{3}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $2x+4x=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $5y-2y=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $a+3a=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $6m-m=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $4x+2y+x=\ansline[1.6cm]$
  \item $x+y=\ansline[1.6cm]$
\end{enumerate}
\end{multicols}

\end{enumerate}

\vspace{4pt}
\ealpara{\ealkeytr{Wyrazy podobne} mają tę samą literę, a zbieramy je, dodając lub odejmując liczby z przodu. \ealkeytr{Pierwiastki niewymierne} zbiera się w ten sam sposób: \ealkeytr{pierwiastek niewymierny} taki jak $\sqrt{3}$ zbiera się tak samo jak litera $x$. \ealkeytr{Pierwiastki niewymierne} z tą samą liczbą pod \ealkeytr{pierwiastkiem}, takie jak $2\sqrt{3}$ i $4\sqrt{3}$, nazywa się \ealkeytr{pierwiastkami podobnymi}. \ealkeytr{Pierwiastek niewymierny} bez liczby z przodu ma $1$ raz, więc $\sqrt{3}=1\sqrt{3}$, tak jak $x=1x$.}{\ealkey{Like terms} have the same letter, and we collect them by adding or subtracting the numbers in front. \ealkey{Surds} are collected in the same way: a \ealkey{surd} such as $\sqrt{3}$ is collected just like the letter $x$. \ealkey{Surds} with the same number under the \ealkey{root}, such as $2\sqrt{3}$ and $4\sqrt{3}$, are called \textbf{\ealkey{like surds}}. A \ealkey{surd} with no number in front has $1$ lot, so $\sqrt{3}=1\sqrt{3}$, just as $x=1x$.}

\begin{formulas}{adding and subtracting \ealkey{like surds}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.9}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{6.6cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$a\sqrt{n}+b\sqrt{n}=(a+b)\sqrt{n}$ & for example \; $2\sqrt{3}+5\sqrt{3}=7\sqrt{3}$\\
$a\sqrt{n}-b\sqrt{n}=(a-b)\sqrt{n}$ & for example \; $9\sqrt{2}-4\sqrt{2}=5\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
\ealpara{Słownie: dodaj lub odejmij liczby z przodu, a \ealkeytr{pierwiastek niewymierny} pozostaw bez zmian.}{In words: add or subtract the numbers in front, and keep the \ealkey{surd} the same.}
\end{formulas}

\begin{warning}
\ealpara{Tylko \ealkeytr{pierwiastki podobne} można zbierać. Tak jak $x+y$ nie można \ealkeytr{uprościć}, tak $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}$ nie można \ealkeytr{uprościć}. To \textbf{nie} jest $\sqrt{5}$: na kalkulatorze $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}=3.146264\ldots$, ale $\sqrt{5}=2.236067\ldots$}{Only \ealkey{like surds} can be collected. Just as $x+y$ cannot be \ealkey{simplified}, $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}$ cannot be \ealkey{simplified}. It is \textbf{not} $\sqrt{5}$: on the calculator $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}=3.146264\ldots$, but $\sqrt{5}=2.236067\ldots$}
\end{warning}

\begin{wex}{collecting \ealkey{like surds}}
\small
\ealpara{Każdy wiersz \ealkeytr{pierwiastków niewymiernych} zbiera się w ten sam sposób co \ealkeytr{algebra} obok.}{Each line of \ealkey{surds} is collected in the same way as the \ealkey{algebra} beside it.}

\smallskip
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{3em}}l@{}}
\textbf{\ealkey{Algebra}} & \textbf{\ealkey{Surds}}\\
$2x+4x=(2+4)x=6x$ & $2\sqrt{3}+4\sqrt{3}=(2+4)\sqrt{3}=6\sqrt{3}$\\
$7y-3y=(7-3)y=4y$ & $7\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2}=(7-3)\sqrt{2}=4\sqrt{2}$\\
$4x+2y+x=5x+2y$ & $4\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}=5\sqrt{2}+2\sqrt{3}$\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}

\parttitle{4}{Multiplying and dividing \ealkey{surds}}

\ealpara{Część 2 pokazała, że $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}$. Czytając w drugą stronę, mówi to, że $\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{18}$: gdy mnożymy dwa \ealkeytr{pierwiastki}, mnożymy liczby pod \ealkeytr{pierwiastkami}. Dzielenie działa w ten sam sposób. Pamiętaj, że $ab$ oznacza $a\times b$.}{Part 2 showed that $\sqrt{18}=\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}$. Read the other way round, this says $\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{18}$: when we multiply two \ealkey{square roots}, we multiply the numbers under the \ealkey{roots}. Dividing works in the same way. Remember that $ab$ means $a\times b$.}

\begin{formulas}{multiplying and dividing \ealkey{surds}}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.95}%
\begin{tabular}{@{}>{\large}p{8.4cm}@{\hspace{1em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{ab}$ & for example \; $\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{6}$\\
$\sqrt{a}\div\sqrt{b}=\sqrt{a\div b}$ \; or \; $\dfrac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{a}{b}}$
  & for example \; $\sqrt{15}\div\sqrt{3}=\sqrt{5}$\\
$\sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{a}=a$ & for example \; $\sqrt{7}\times\sqrt{7}=7$\\
$m\sqrt{a}\times n\sqrt{b}=mn\sqrt{ab}$ & for example \; $2\sqrt{3}\times4\sqrt{5}=8\sqrt{15}$\\
$m\sqrt{a}\div n\sqrt{b}=(m\div n)\sqrt{a\div b}$ & for example \; $8\sqrt{6}\div2\sqrt{3}=4\sqrt{2}$\\
\end{tabular}

\vspace{4pt}
\ealpara{Słownie: pomnóż lub podziel liczby pod \ealkeytr{pierwiastkami}. Liczby z przodu mnoży się lub dzieli osobno.}{In words: multiply or divide the numbers under the \ealkey{roots}. Numbers in front are multiplied or divided separately.}
\end{formulas}

\begin{wex}{multiplying \ealkey{surds}}
\small
\ealpara{Odpowiedź może być \ealkeytr{liczbą całkowitą nieujemną}. Liczby z przodu są mnożone osobno.}{the answer can be a \ealkey{whole number}; the numbers in front are multiplied separately.}
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}l@{\hspace{2em}}l@{}}
$\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{3\times5}=\sqrt{15}$ & \\
$\sqrt{2}\times\sqrt{8}=\sqrt{2\times8}=\sqrt{16}=4$
  & the answer can be a \ealkey{whole number}\\
$2\sqrt{3}\times4\sqrt{5}=(2\times4)\sqrt{3\times5}=8\sqrt{15}$
  & the numbers in front are multiplied separately\\
\end{tabular}
\end{wex}

(b) $2\sqrt{3}\times5\sqrt{2}=10\sqrt{6}$ cm$^2$ \quad
(c) $\sqrt{35}\div\sqrt{5}=\sqrt{7}$ cm

\textbf{Q11.} (a) $\sqrt{2}+4\sqrt{2}$; \; $8\sqrt{2}-3\sqrt{2}$; \;
$\sqrt{25}\times\sqrt{2}$; \; $10\sqrt{6}\div2\sqrt{3}$; \; $\sqrt{50}$.
\quad Parts (b) to (e) have many answers. For example:
(b) $4\sqrt{5}-\sqrt{5}$; \; $\sqrt{9}\times\sqrt{5}$; \;
$6\sqrt{10}\div2\sqrt{2}$. \quad
(c) $2\sqrt{2}+4\sqrt{2}$; \; $7\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}$; \;
$\sqrt{36}\times\sqrt{2}$; \; $12\sqrt{6}\div2\sqrt{3}$; \; $\sqrt{72}$.
\quad
(d) $\sqrt{7}+\sqrt{7}$; \; $5\sqrt{7}-3\sqrt{7}$; \;
$\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{7}$; \; $6\sqrt{14}\div3\sqrt{2}$; \; $\sqrt{28}$.
\quad (e) Any \ealkey{surd}, with five calculations that give it.
